No alternative diagnosis (e.g., placental abruption, vasa previa, or cervical laceration) explains *all* findings: abruption would typically show retroplacental clot on ultrasound (not described), lack scar-site discontinuity, and often present with uterine hyperstimulation/hypertonus — none of which are mentioned. Vasa previa would cause painless bleeding and fetal bradycardia, not variable decels or abdominal pain. Cervical/vaginal trauma would not cause hemoperitoneum or ultrasound-confirmed uterine wall disruption. Thus, uterine rupture is not only consistent but uniquely explained by the totality of evidence.

[EVIDENCE]  
- 38-week gestational age with prior cesarean delivery (implied by “prior cesarean scar”)  
- Acute-onset vaginal bleeding  
- Severe abdominal pain  
- Recurrent variable decelerations on fetal monitoring  
- Ultrasound shows disruption of uterine wall continuity at prior cesarean scar site  
- Ultrasound shows associated hemoperitoneum  
- Maternal tachycardia (pulse 110/min)  
- Maternal hypotension (BP 90/60 mm Hg)  
- Mild anemia (hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL), consistent with acute blood loss  
- Normal coagulation parameters (PT 11 sec, aPTT 30 sec), arguing against consumptive coagulopathy and supporting isolated hemorrhage  

[GAPS]  
- Exact timing of prior cesarean delivery (e.g., interval since last cesarean) — relevant for rupture risk stratification but not required for diagnosis  
- Quantitative blood loss estimate — clinically inferred but not measured  
- Fetal pH or Apgar scores — not yet obtained due to emergent context  
- None of these gaps undermine the diagnosis; ultrasound + clinical triad is diagnostic  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Uterine rupture
